course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 7

unit.title: Food Chains and Food Webs
unit.blurb: Microorganisms and decomposition, and how energy passes along food chains and food webs – including what happens when one species changes.

O1.t: Describe microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protists), where they live, and helpful and harmful examples.

O2.t: Describe the role of microorganisms as decomposers that recycle nutrients.

O3.t: Construct and interpret food chains and food webs, including producers, consumers and decomposers.

O4.t: Predict how a change to one population (or human impacts such as microplastics) affects a food web.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 5: Food Chains and Food Webs.
We will discover how energy passes from one living thing to another,
and why tiny microorganisms that break down dead matter are so important.
Every food chain starts with something that makes its own food.
In the ocean, tiny producers make food from sunlight.
Small fish eat them, bigger fish eat the small fish,
seals eat the bigger fish, and sharks eat the seals.
Sadly, tiny pieces of plastic called microplastics also travel up food chains.
Shrimp eat them by mistake, jellyfish eat the shrimp,
and turtles eat the jellyfish.
Microplastics can even end up in the food we eat.
Why does food go mouldy when it is left out?
Because of microorganisms. Micro means very small, and organism means a living thing.
Most are just one cell, so we need a microscope to see them.
There are different kinds.
Bacteria are single cells found almost everywhere, and moulds are tiny fungi.
Protists include algae, which can photosynthesise, and amoebae, which cannot.
When millions grow together they form a colony,
like the mould on old bread.
A colony is big enough to see without a microscope.
Microorganisms live everywhere: in soil, in plants, in fresh, salty and brackish water,
on and inside animals' bodies, and in waste.
Many are helpful. Bacteria in your gut help break down food,
bacteria in your nose stop harmful microbes getting in,
and skin bacteria help fight infection.
Others are unhelpful. Mouth bacteria cause tooth decay and bad breath,
and fungi can cause athlete's foot and dandruff.
A microorganism that causes disease is called a pathogen.
Three slices of the same bread are kept for five days.
A is damp and warm.
B is damp but in a fridge.
C is dry and warm.
Predict: which slice will grow the most mould?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Each slice is sealed in a bag so nothing else can get in,
and left for five days.
Slice A, damp and warm, is covered in mould.
Slice B, in the fridge, has only a little.
Slice C, dry, has none.
Explain what you saw.
Mould is a fungus, a microorganism that feeds on the bread and grows.
Microorganisms grow fastest when it is warm and moist.
Cold slows them down, and without water they cannot grow.
That is why we keep food in a fridge,
or dry it to make it last longer.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Have you noticed how dead leaves under a tree slowly disappear?
Let's follow what happens.
Living plants grow using mineral salts from the soil.
When leaves and plants die, they fall to the ground.
Microorganisms feed on the dead matter.
As they feed and respire, they break it down into simpler substances.
This is called decomposition.
Decomposition releases mineral salts into the soil, which plants absorb through their roots.
It works just like a recycling system!
The microorganisms that break down dead matter are called decomposers.
Scientists put dead rainforest leaves into net bags and left them outside for nine months,
measuring their mass from time to time.
After one month, the mass had fallen by 20 percent.
After three months, it had fallen by 45 percent.
After nine months, the leaves had lost 70 percent of their mass.
Decomposers were breaking them down.
Here, the independent variable is time,
and the dependent variable is the mass of the leaves.
Control variables include the type of leaves,
the bags and the place they were left.
Can you predict what would happen after a year?
An ecosystem is all the living and non-living parts of an area,
like this forest. Non-living parts include sunlight, rain, temperature, air, water and soil.
The organisms interact. Animals rely on plants for food and shelter, and plants need light,
carbon dioxide, water and soil.
Decomposers, such as bacteria and fungi, clear away animal wastes and dead organisms,
stopping waste from building up and recycling nutrients.
Worms and many insects, called detritivores,
help by breaking dead matter into smaller pieces.
Only energy needs to come from outside, as light from the Sun.

captions: All living things need energy, which usually comes from food.
A food chain is a model that shows how
energy passes from one organism to the next.
Here: seaweed, fish, seal, shark.
The arrows in a food chain mean is eaten by.
The seaweed is eaten by the fish,
the fish is eaten by the seal, and so on.
So the arrows point in the direction that energy flows through the ecosystem.
Look at this leaf.
It takes in sunlight, carbon dioxide from the air,
and water from the soil, and gives out oxygen.
This is photosynthesis. Using light energy, trapped by green chlorophyll in chloroplasts,
the plant turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose, its food,
and releases oxygen.
An organism that makes its own food is a producer.
Plants and algae are producers, and every food chain starts with one.
All the other organisms depend on it.
Not all producers look green!
The copper beech tree has red leaves because red pigments hide its chlorophyll,
but it still photosynthesises.
Animals cannot make their own food.
They must eat other organisms, so they are called consumers.
Consumers are grouped by what they eat.
Herbivores eat plants, and carnivores eat other animals.
Omnivores eat both plants and animals.
Consumers can also be predators, which hunt, or prey, which are hunted.
A lion is a predator and a zebra is its prey.
Humans eat plants and animals, so we are omnivores.
Let's follow the energy in a mangrove forest.
The mangrove plants are the producers.
They trap energy from sunlight and store some in the materials they are made of.
A crab eats the mangrove leaves.
Energy and nutrients pass from the plants to the crab.
A kingfisher eats the crab, so energy passes to the kingfisher.
Then a python eats the kingfisher, and the energy passes on again.
Energy and nutrients travel along food chains, and so do microplastics.
They have even been found in penguins in Antarctica!
Rice fields are full of life.
Let's build a real food chain, step by step,
from the energy in sunlight.
Rice plants are the producers.
They trap the Sun's energy and make food by photosynthesis.
Grasshoppers eat the rice leaves.
They are herbivores and primary consumers.
Frogs eat the grasshoppers, so they are secondary consumers.
Herons eat the frogs.
They are tertiary consumers, at the top of this chain.
So the chain is: rice, grasshopper, frog, heron.
Pause and decide: what would happen to the rice if
a farmer sprayed poison that killed all the frogs?
We can name each organism by its position in the chain.
In the ocean, phytoplankton are the producers.
They bring energy into the chain by photosynthesis.
Zooplankton eat the producer, so they are the primary consumers.
The fish eats the zooplankton, so it is a secondary consumer.
The shark eats the fish, so it is a tertiary consumer.
An animal that eats a tertiary consumer is a quaternary consumer.
And at every level, decomposers break down wastes and dead organisms.
Let's build a food chain from some forest organisms, using these clues.
Always start with the producer.
The Bengal bamboo makes its own food, so it goes first.
What eats the bamboo?
The giant squirrel is a herbivore, so it comes next.
The pit viper is both predator and prey,
so it must eat the squirrel and be eaten by something else.
The crested serpent eagle is only a predator,
so it goes at the end: bamboo, squirrel, pit viper, eagle.
Simple food chains are rare in nature.
A frog, for example, doesn't eat just one thing.
It eats flies, grasshoppers, spiders and even earthworms.
And spiders eat flies too!
So the food chains link together and overlap.
When we join all the food chains in an ecosystem,
we get a food web.
It shows all the feeding relationships, and an animal can be a primary,
secondary and tertiary consumer at the same time.
Here is a small food web.
Predict: if all the frogs died from a disease,
what would happen to the number of grasshoppers?
Pause and decide.
Watch. A disease kills all the frogs.
They are removed from the web.
With no frogs eating them, the number of grasshoppers increases.
The eagles have fewer frogs, so they eat more rabbits.
More grasshoppers eat more grass,
so there is less grass for the rabbits and mice.
Explain what you saw.
In a food web, every organism is linked.
Removing one species changes the food supply of its predators and its prey.
Its prey increase, and its predators switch to other food.
One change ripples through the whole web.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Food webs can be read like a map.
Ask yourself: which organisms are producers?
Which is an omnivore?
Which is both a primary and a secondary consumer?
Think about what would happen if one species disappeared.
Its predators would have less food, and its prey might increase.
One change can ripple through the whole web.
Decomposers belong in food webs too.
Bacteria and fungi break down dead organisms and wastes from every level,
and some animals even feed on the decomposers.
Scientists are developing biodegradable plastics made from plants, such as PLA,
which decomposers can break down into water and carbon dioxide.
In 2022, enormous swarms of jellyfish arrived on Mediterranean coasts.
Climate change has warmed the sea, so jellyfish breed and grow more quickly.
This changes ocean food webs.
More jellyfish eat more phytoplankton, leaving less food for small fish,
and fewer fish for whales, seals and seabirds.
But turtles and sunfish, which eat jellyfish, get more food.
The swarms also cause problems for people: they scare tourists,
clog fishing nets and block water pipes.
Scientists are testing solutions,
but working together to limit climate change is the most important step.
Now it is your turn to shine!
Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What do the arrows in a food chain show?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The direction energy flows – “is eaten by”.
Question 2: Termites eat banana leaves, chameleons eat termites, pythons eat chameleons.
Write the food chain.
Pause the video now.
Answer: banana leaves → termites → chameleons → pythons.
Question 3: What is the main source of energy for a food chain?
Pause the video now.
Answer: Light from the Sun, trapped by producers in photosynthesis.
Question 4: Why are decomposers important?
Pause the video now.
Answer: They break down dead matter and wastes,
recycling mineral salts back into the soil.
